Growing guide · Courgettes and Marrows
Warmth and moisture drive growth.

Plant after frost and avoid cold, wet starts or drought checks.

Pick courgettes frequently.

Young tender fruits keep plants cropping; mature marrows are a different use.

Soil & preparation
Use a warm, sunny, sheltered site with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Prepare compost-rich planting pockets.
Mulch generously and leave enough room for the chosen bush or trailing type. Avoid poorly drained ground.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow on edge

Sow singly in warm pots or modules, with the seed on edge. Keep compost lightly moist; cold, wet compost can rot the seed.

2 Keep one strong plant

Harden off and plant after frost risk. For direct sowing in warm soil, sow two or three per station and keep the strongest.

Sow indoors in warmth in late April; plant after frost risk. Direct sowing is safer in warm late-May–June soil. Temporary fleece helps establishment.

Looking after the crop
Water deeply at the roots and mulch with compost for steady growth. Avoid prolonged leaf wetness. A midsummer compost dressing sustains large leaves and fruit production.
Allow pollinators access. If fruit set is poor, transfer pollen from a male flower to the centre of a female flower, which has a small fruit behind it.
Use strong supports for trailing marrows, tying stems gently. Support heavy fruit separately; restrict unwanted extension if needed.
Harvesting & storage
Cut young courgettes, often 4–6 in. long, daily or every other day in warmth. Leave a short stem; do not snap off. Remove misshapen first fruits promptly. Overgrown fruit slows further cropping.
Pick marrows tender for immediate use, or let selected storage fruits develop hard skins before frost. Handle gently and keep dry.
Discard unusually bitter fruit. Wear gloves or long sleeves if stems irritate your skin; flowers can also be used in the kitchen.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
SLUGS	Young plants are chewed.	Protect establishment; inspect and hand-pick in damp weather.
MILDEW	White powder on older leaves.	Keep roots moist; remove badly affected leaves as needed.
POOR POLLINATION	Fruitlets yellow, wither or fail to swell.	Allow insect access; hand-pollinate where necessary.
FRUIT ROT	Fruit softens where it touches wet ground.	Lift onto a clean support; remove rotten fruit.
Cucumber Mosaic Virus	Mottled, puckered leaves; stunted growth.	Remove infected plants; clear weed hosts and monitor aphids.
Bitterness	Fruit tastes unusually bitter.	Discard bitter fruit; do not try to make it safe by cooking.
Root Rot	Wilting; dark, decaying roots.	Remove collapsed plants; improve drainage and avoid cold wet roots.
Final tips

Raise developing marrows on a clean tile or board to keep their skins dry and sound.

Remove misshapen first fruits and keep picking young courgettes to encourage the next crop.

Medium
3/5

Summer / Autumn

Tomato plants are found in the majority of greenhouses during summer, producing a succession of fruit from early summer into autumn. They need constant care: water growing bags or pots regularly in summer and watch for pests and diseases. Home growers can choose flavours and varieties that are rarely sold commercially. Tall or cordon plants are trained with one central stem and their side-shoots removed throughout the season. They need warmth, light, steady root moisture, good ventilation and balanced fertility more than sheer feeding.

8–11 days

8 lb

Recommended varieties
CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sungold F1

A vigorous cordon tomato with very sweet orange cherry fruits. A strong first choice for greenhouse snacking and salads.

ORDINARY
Alicante

A traditional red salad tomato grown as a cordon. Retain as an accessible, general-purpose greenhouse variety.

F1 HYBRID
Shirley

An early cordon tomato producing medium red fruits under glass. A familiar, practical choice for an unheated greenhouse.

CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sweet Million F1

A cordon tomato producing many small red cherry fruits. Complements orange Sungold with a familiar red-fruited alternative.

NOVELTY
San Marzano

A plum tomato for sauces and cooking. Give it warm protected conditions and distinguish it from fresh-eating cherry selections.

Key risks
BLIGHT

Tomato blight causes brown lesions on leaves and stems, followed by fruit decay and plant collapse in favourable damp conditions.

Greenhouse Whitefly

Whitefly adults and immature stages suck sap; sticky honeydew can support black sooty mould.

Blossom End Rot

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.

SPLIT FRUIT

Irregular watering, particularly soaking after severe drying, can split ripe fruit.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
82

Growing guide · Tomato, Greenhouse
Water steadily and ventilate.

Even root moisture and moving air help fruit develop without splits or mould.

Train to the variety’s habit.

Remove side shoots from cordons; bush types need a different routine.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained border soil with compost, or suitable pots/growbags of fresh peat-free compost.
Avoid waterlogging and stale, humid air. Containers need closer watering and feeding than a well-prepared border.
Looking after the crop
Tie cordons loosely; remove young side shoots. Take yellow lower leaves sparingly; keep healthy leaves to feed and shade fruit. Stop two leaves above the final truss at the chosen height or near season’s end. Bush and semi-determinate pruning differs.
Water roots steadily; feed organically at the product rate as fruit develops. Ventilate in heat and gently tap flowering trusses. Match autumn watering to growth.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently; use promptly. Before cold ends the crop, bring sound unripe fruit indoors. Ripen at room temperature, checking trays for decay; a nearby ripe apple or banana can help.
Sowing & planting
1 Grow on in a pot

Sow in trays or small pots; keep compost moist, not wet. Prick out and pot on as needed. Bright light gives stout seedlings.

2 Plant and support

In a warm greenhouse, water well-rooted plants before setting slightly deeper in pots, growbags or beds. Support cordons with canes or string.

Pots / growbags One plant per 12–18 in. diameter pot; two per standard growbag. Use peat-free compost.
Pot spacing Upright cordons: about 24 in. between pot centres for foliage space.
Soil beds Plants 18–24 in. apart in compost-enriched soil; wider for vigorous cordons and airflow.

For unheated cover, sow around March in gentle warmth near 68°F. Earlier heated crops need reliable warmth and bright winter light.

Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
BLIGHT — Brown leaf lesions; fruit may rot.	Remove infected plants; keep leaves dry and ventilate.
Greenhouse Whitefly — White flies; sticky leaves and sooty mould.	Identify early; use suitable biological control.
Blossom End Rot — Dark leathery patch at fruit base.	Keep roots evenly moist, especially as fruit swells.
SPLIT FRUIT — Skins crack after uneven watering.	Keep moisture steady; avoid drying then flooding.
Tomato Leaf Mould — Yellow patches above; brown mould below.	Remove infected leaves; ventilate; keep foliage dry.
Aphids — Colonies on young growth.	Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones; encourage predators.
Grey Mould (Botrytis) — Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.	Remove infected tissue and dead material; ventilate.
Blossom Drop — Flowers wither and fall without setting.	Water steadily; ventilate in heat; gently tap trusses.
Virus — Leaves mottled and distorted; plants stunted.	Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools; monitor aphids.
Magnesium Deficiency — Lower leaves yellow between green veins.	Check watering, pH and feed; avoid excess potash.
Final tips

Check leaf undersides often; manage whitefly while numbers are low.

Avoid excess high-potash feed: nutrient balance matters as much as quantity.

VEGETABLE GUIDES

Stalks & Shoots
Asparagus.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer

Asparagus is one of the finest spring vegetables: a long-lived perennial which gives a fresh, delicate crop just when the garden is short of new green shoots. It is not difficult once established, but it asks for space, clean ground and patience. Treat the bed as a permanent feature: clear perennial weeds thoroughly, improve the soil before planting and do not crop hard while the crowns are young. In return, a good bed can produce spears for many years, followed by tall ferny summer growth which feeds the roots for the next season.

Recommended varieties
Gijnlim

An early, all-male hybrid producing green spears. A strong first choice for a productive, permanent asparagus bed.

Connover's Colossal

A long-established asparagus with substantial green spears. Keep as the traditional alternative to modern all-male hybrids.

Backlim

An all-male hybrid cropping later than early selections. Plant alongside an earlier variety to spread the asparagus harvest.

Key risks
VIOLET ROOT ROT

Purple fungal growth on roots, with yellowing and dying fern, can indicate violet root rot.

FROST

Young shoots may turn black and die if a severe frost occurs in late spring.

PERENNIAL WEEDS

Couch grass, bindweed and other perennial weeds are a serious long-term problem in asparagus beds.

SLUGS

Spears are gnawed, making them unfit for table use.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
88

Growing guide · Asparagus
Good drainage is essential.

Choose a sunny, sheltered site and enrich the soil with compost or well-rotted manure.

Clear perennial weeds before planting.

A light-excluding mulch for a whole season is worthwhile on badly infested ground.

Plant crowns in early spring.

Delay if the soil is cold and wet; keep bought crowns moist.

Soil & preparation
Choose sunny, sheltered, well-drained soil. Add compost or rotted manure; lime very acid ground if needed. Improve heavy-ground drainage or use a raised bed.
Clear perennial weeds first: their roots are hard to remove once tangled with crowns.
Sowing & planting
1 Prepare a mound

Keep crowns moist. Mound fine soil in the clean, well-drained trench.

2 Spread the roots

Spread roots over the mound, with the crown above the root ends.

3 Cover the roots

Cover roots; leave bud tips visible. Water to settle; keep mulch off growth points.

Trench Dig 12 in. wide and 8 in. deep; centres 18 in. apart. Stagger plants in adjacent trenches.
Initial cover Cover roots; leave bud tips visible

From seed: sow thinly in spring, thin and grow on. Plant into the final bed next spring; cropping starts later than with crowns.

Looking after the crop
Hand-weed or hoe shallowly to protect roots. Water in dry spells, especially while plants establish. Mulch mature beds against weeds, keeping growth points clear. Strong summer ferns build next spring’s reserves.
Each year, mulch established beds with 1–2 in. of compost or well-rotted manure. Tidy and lightly feed with compost before spears appear.
Support tall ferns if needed. Remove berries before they fall and seed into the bed. Let ferns yellow before cutting down; remove diseased growth.
Harvesting & storage
Wait two years after planting crowns, or three years from seed. Let uncut spears form fern to build strong roots.
Cut finger-thick spears by 7 in. tall, about 1 in. below soil, before they turn woody. Use a sharp knife, avoiding nearby shoots. Check every few days in cool weather, daily in warmth.
Cut for six weeks in the first harvest year, then up to eight weeks. Stop by mid-June, sooner if weak, and let later spears form fern.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
VIOLET ROOT ROT	Roots develop purple mould; foliage yellows and dies.	Confirm diagnosis; remove affected crowns and replant on clean ground.
FROST	Young shoots turn black and die after late spring frost.	Remove damaged shoots and cover the bed if hard frost is forecast.
PERENNIAL WEEDS	Couch, bindweed and other perennial weeds invade the crowns.	Clear them before planting; later removal risks crop damage.
SLUGS	Spears are gnawed and become unfit to eat.	Check shoots on damp evenings, hand-pick slugs and encourage natural predators.
Final tips

Treat the bed as a permanent feature: clean ground and patience pay off.

Strong summer fern growth feeds the crowns for next spring.

Troubles

Downy Mildew
RECOGNISE

Grey mould develops on onion leaves after wet weather, sometimes followed by black sootiness. Growth and storage quality suffer.

ACT

Remove badly affected material. Dry harvested bulbs thoroughly and keep suspect bulbs out of long storage.

Rotate, space well and improve drainage. Avoid nearby overwintered infected onions; choose resistant varieties.

RECOGNISE

Caterpillars feed inside leaves, leaving translucent patches or shredded tissue. Unlike fly maggots, they have heads and small legs.

RECOGNISE

Yellowing leaves accompany root and bulb-base decay, white fungal fluff and tiny black resting bodies.

ACT

No cure: remove diseased plants and keep contaminated soil off clean ground.

PREVENT

Do not rely on normal rotation: resting bodies can survive at least 15 years. Grow alliums in clean ground.

Shanking
RECOGNISE

RECOGNISE

Check stores regularly and discard rotting bulbs immediately.

Remove badly infested plants and debris; internal larvae are hard to reach.

Use fine mesh and rotation, especially during adult activity in March-April and September-November.

Growing guide · Courgettes and Marrows
Warmth and moisture drive growth.

Plant after frost and avoid cold, wet starts or drought checks.

Pick courgettes frequently.

Young tender fruits keep plants cropping; mature marrows are a different use.

Soil & preparation
Use a warm, sunny, sheltered site with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Prepare compost-rich planting pockets.
Mulch generously and leave enough room for the chosen bush or trailing type. Avoid poorly drained ground.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow on edge

Sow singly in warm pots or modules, with the seed on edge. Keep compost lightly moist; cold, wet compost can rot the seed.

2 Keep one strong plant

Harden off and plant after frost risk. For direct sowing in warm soil, sow two or three per station and keep the strongest.

Sow indoors in warmth in late April; plant after frost risk. Direct sowing is safer in warm late-May–June soil. Temporary fleece helps establishment.

Looking after the crop
Water deeply at the roots and mulch with compost for steady growth. Avoid prolonged leaf wetness. A midsummer compost dressing sustains large leaves and fruit production.

Use strong supports for trailing marrows, tying stems gently. Support heavy fruit separately; restrict unwanted extension if needed.

Discard unusually bitter fruit. Wear gloves or long sleeves if stems irritate your skin; flowers can also be used in the kitchen.

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.

Irregular watering, particularly soaking after severe drying, can split ripe fruit.

Water steadily and ventilate.

Even root moisture and moving air help fruit develop without splits or mould.

Train to the variety’s habit.

Remove side shoots from cordons; bush types need a different routine.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained border soil with compost, or suitable pots/growbags of fresh peat-free compost.
Avoid waterlogging and stale, humid air. Containers need closer watering and feeding than a well-prepared border.
Looking after the crop
Tie cordons loosely; remove young side shoots. Take yellow lower leaves sparingly; keep healthy leaves to feed and shade fruit. Stop two leaves above the final truss at the chosen height or near season’s end. Bush and semi-determinate pruning differs.

1 Grow on in a pot

In a warm greenhouse, water well-rooted plants before setting slightly deeper in pots, growbags or beds. Support cordons with canes or string.

HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer

Asparagus is one of the finest spring vegetables: a long-lived perennial which gives a fresh, delicate crop just when the garden is short of new green shoots. It is not difficult once established, but it asks for space, clean ground and patience. Recommended varieties

An early, all-male hybrid producing green spears. A strong first choice for a productive, permanent asparagus bed.

Connover's Colossal

A long-established asparagus with substantial green spears. Keep as the traditional alternative to modern all-male hybrids.

VIOLET ROOT ROT

Purple fungal growth on roots, with yellowing and dying fern, can indicate violet root rot.

FROST

Young shoots may turn black and die if a severe frost occurs in late spring.

PERENNIAL WEEDS

Couch grass, bindweed and other perennial weeds are a serious long-term problem in asparagus beds.

88

Growing guide · Asparagus
Good drainage is essential.

Choose a sunny, sheltered site and enrich the soil with compost or well-rotted manure.

Clear perennial weeds before planting.

A light-excluding mulch for a whole season is worthwhile on badly infested ground.

Plant crowns in early spring.

Delay if the soil is cold and wet; keep bought crowns moist.

Soil & preparation
Choose sunny, sheltered, well-drained soil. Add compost or rotted manure; lime very acid ground if needed. Improve heavy-ground drainage or use a raised bed.
Clear perennial weeds first: their roots are hard to remove once tangled with crowns.
Sowing & planting
1 Prepare a mound

Keep crowns moist. Mound fine soil in the clean, well-drained trench.

2 Spread the roots

Spread roots over the mound, with the crown above the root ends.

3 Cover the roots

Cover roots; leave bud tips visible. Water to settle; keep mulch off growth points.

Trench Dig 30 cm wide and 20 cm deep; centres 45 cm apart. Stagger plants in adjacent trenches.
Initial cover Cover roots; leave bud tips visible

From seed: sow thinly in spring, thin and grow on. Plant into the final bed next spring; cropping starts later than with crowns.

Looking after the crop
Hand-weed or hoe shallowly to protect roots. Water in dry spells, especially while plants establish. Mulch mature beds against weeds, keeping growth points clear. Strong summer ferns build next spring’s reserves.
Each year, mulch established beds with 2.5–5 cm of compost or well-rotted manure. Tidy and lightly feed with compost before spears appear.
Support tall ferns if needed. Remove berries before they fall and seed into the bed. Let ferns yellow before cutting down; remove diseased growth.
Harvesting & storage
Wait two years after planting crowns, or three years from seed. Let uncut spears form fern to build strong roots.
Cut finger-thick spears by 18 cm tall, about 2.5 cm below soil, before they turn woody. Use a sharp knife, avoiding nearby shoots. Check every few days in cool weather, daily in warmth.
Cut for six weeks in the first harvest year, then up to eight weeks. Stop by mid-June, sooner if weak, and let later spears form fern.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
VIOLET ROOT ROT	Roots develop purple mould; foliage yellows and dies.	Confirm diagnosis; remove affected crowns and replant on clean ground.
FROST	Young shoots turn black and die after late spring frost.	Remove damaged shoots and cover the bed if hard frost is forecast.

SLUGS	Spears are gnawed and become unfit to eat.	Check shoots on damp evenings, hand-pick slugs and encourage natural predators.

Treat the bed as a permanent feature: clean ground and patience pay off.

Strong summer fern growth feeds the crowns for next spring.

Onion & Leek
Troubles

Check alliums at the leaf base as well as above ground. Feeding damage, rot and growth checks can look alike. Use sound bulbs with thick necks or splits promptly; store only dry, healthy bulbs. White rot needs particular care to avoid spreading soil.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Bolting
RECOGNISE

A premature flower stalk forms, often after cold or checked growth. Oversized sets can be more susceptible.

ACT

Pinch out small flower stems without loosening bulbs; use affected bulbs early.

PREVENT

Choose suitable small or heat-treated sets, plant at the recommended season and avoid growth checks.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Saddleback

Bulbs split at base.

RECOGNISE

Bulbs split at the base, often after heavy rain or watering follows prolonged drought.

ACT

Use sound split bulbs promptly; they will not store well.

PREVENT

Keep growth steady with watering during dry summer spells.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Set Division
RECOGNISE

Onion sets may form twin bulbs; large sets and growth checks can contribute. Shallots naturally form clusters.

PREVENT

Use suitable onion sets, plant in season and maintain steady growth. Shallot division is normal.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Birds Pulling Sets

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out of the soil just as they begin to grow.

RECOGNISE

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out before they establish. Birds may investigate their exposed dry tips.

ACT

Replant sound lifted sets promptly before their roots dry out.

PREVENT

Firm sets at normal depth and guard with secure netting until rooted. Check for trapped wildlife.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Onion Fly

Tunnelled bulbs with 0.6 cm white maggots.

RECOGNISE

Yellow, drooping leaves accompany maggots feeding at bulb bases. Seedlings may die; older plants fail to develop.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants and infested bulbs.

PREVENT

Use insect-proof mesh with rotation. Clear crop debris; sets are less vulnerable than seedlings.

VEGETABLE TROUBLES
126

Onion & Leek
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Drooping Leaves
RECOGNISE

Dark-green leaves may flop after excessive nitrogen. But drooping alone also needs checks for watering problems, pests or normal maturity.

ACT

Check roots and bulb bases before assuming a feeding problem.

PREVENT

Avoid fresh manure and excessive nitrogen; do not add fertiliser blindly.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

Stem & Bulb Eelworm

Twisted, swollen leaves.

RECOGNISE

Swollen, distorted leaves accompany soft bulbs. Microscopic stem and bulb nematodes may kill young plants.

ACT

Remove affected plants and seek a confirmed diagnosis.

PREVENT

Avoid moving infested soil. Plan a suitable rotation for the identified nematode and its host range.

LEEK

Smut
RECOGNISE

Black spots and blotches develop on leaves or bulbs of young plants; leaves thicken and twist. Leeks are particularly vulnerable.

ACT

Remove affected plants and seek confirmation.

PREVENT

Avoid moving affected soil and seek advice on a long crop break; the fungus can persist for years.

LEEK / GARLIC

Rust
RECOGNISE

Orange pustules mark leek and garlic leaves. Often cosmetic, heavy attacks yellow foliage and check growth.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves and keep plants growing steadily.

PREVENT

Avoid crowding and excess nitrogen; water roots in dry spells and clear infected debris.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Bull Neck (Thick Neck)
RECOGNISE

Onions retain unusually thick, fleshy necks and store poorly. Excess nitrogen or deep sowing may contribute.

ACT

Use sound affected bulbs early; do not store them with well-ripened bulbs.

PREVENT

Avoid overfeeding and deep sowing. Additional feed will not cure a thick neck.

LEEK

White Tip
RECOGNISE

Leek tips turn white and papery in autumn; damage spreads down leaves and may stunt growth.

ACT

Remove badly diseased plants and affected debris.

PREVENT

Avoid an affected bed the following season; improve drainage and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.

VEGETABLE TROUBLES
127

Onion & Leek
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Downy Mildew
RECOGNISE

Grey mould develops on onion leaves after wet weather, sometimes followed by black sootiness. Growth and storage quality suffer.

ACT

Remove badly affected material. Dry harvested bulbs thoroughly and keep suspect bulbs out of long storage.

PREVENT

Rotate, space well and improve drainage. Avoid nearby overwintered infected onions; choose resistant varieties.

LEEK / ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / GARLIC

Leek Moth
RECOGNISE

Caterpillars feed inside leaves, leaving translucent patches or shredded tissue. Unlike fly maggots, they have heads and small legs.

ACT

Remove infested leaves. Badly damaged leeks may regrow if cut about 5 cm / 2 in above soil; remove the debris.

PREVENT

Protect young plants with fine mesh from planting out, using a rotated bed.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS / LEEK / GARLIC

White Rot (Mouldy Nose)
RECOGNISE

Yellowing leaves accompany root and bulb-base decay, white fungal fluff and tiny black resting bodies.

ACT

No cure: remove diseased plants and keep contaminated soil off clean ground.

PREVENT

Do not rely on normal rotation: resting bodies can survive at least 15 years. Grow alliums in clean ground.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Shanking
RECOGNISE

Yellowing, collapsing leaves and foul-smelling slime inside onion scales suggest soft rot.

ACT

Remove rotten bulbs promptly; keep them out of storage.

Saddleback

Bulbs split at base.

RECOGNISE

Bulbs split at the base, often after heavy rain or watering follows prolonged drought.

ACT

Use sound split bulbs promptly; they will not store well.

Keep growth steady with watering during dry summer spells.

Set Division
RECOGNISE

Onion sets may form twin bulbs; large sets and growth checks can contribute. Shallots naturally form clusters.

PREVENT

ACT
